desc:
The string s is a valid infix expression: single lowercase letters are operands, +, -, *, / are binary operators (* and / bind tighter than + and -, and operators of equal priority are applied from left to right), and round brackets group sub-expressions. There are no unary operators and no spaces.

A pair of matching brackets is redundant if deleting just this one pair (leaving all other characters unchanged) gives an expression that is read in exactly the same way, i.e. with the same operation tree. For example in (a+b)+c the brackets are redundant because a+b+c is also read as (a+b)+c, but in a+(b+c) they are not. Brackets around a single letter or around another bracket pair are redundant too.

Return the number of redundant bracket pairs. Each pair is judged on its own.

Examples: ((a+b)) has 2, (a*b)+c has 1, (a+b)*c has 0, (a/b)*(c/d) has 1 (only the first pair).
constraints: s contains lowercase letters, + - * / and round brackets, and is a valid expression
Brackets can be nested up to 4,000 levels deep
hints: Look at one bracket pair at a time. What decides whether the brackets matter is the operator just outside on the left, the operator just outside on the right, and the operators directly inside (not inside deeper brackets).

Use a stack of open brackets and, for each open bracket, remember the lowest priority among the operators that appear directly at its own level. If there is no such operator, the pair only wraps a single operand or another pair.

Let m be that lowest inner priority, L the operator right before the ( (none if there is none or the previous character is another () and R the operator right after the ) (none if absent or the next character is )). The pair is redundant if there is no inner operator, or prio(L) < m (or no L) and prio(R) <= m (or no R).
editorial: Removing a pair changes the reading only if one of the neighbouring operators would now grab part of the bracket's content. Only the operators at the top level of the pair matter, because deeper ones stay protected by their own brackets, and among those only the one with the lowest priority m (those bind loosest and are the most exposed).

On the left side, an operator L in front of the pair would swallow the first operand of the contents if prio(L) >= m (equal priority is also a problem: a-(b-c) would turn into (a-b)-c). So we need prio(L) < m. On the right side, an operator R would steal the last operand if prio(R) > m; for prio(R) == m everything is left-associative, so (a-b)-c and a-b-c mean the same, and equal priority is fine. A neighbour that is a bracket or the string boundary (the next outer pair protects us) cannot interfere. A pair with no top-level operator is always redundant.

Scan once with a stack. On ( push the position and a minimum initialised to infinity. On an operator update the minimum of the top frame (operators outside every bracket are ignored). On ) pop the frame, look at the characters right before the open bracket and right after this close bracket, and apply the rule. Time O(n), space O(n).
